name: Real-time Collaboration
tagline: Chat, presence and shared documents where latency is the product
summary: Stateful connection servers in front of a fan-out layer, with a durable log behind them. The hard parts are not the transport but connection state, ordering and what happens when a server or a network blips.
basis: TechFlow archetype, not a specific company's stack. It reflects the shape most chat and collaboration systems converge on once one server can no longer hold every connection.

items.note: Bidirectional messages; reconnect with backoff and replay from a cursor.
Simpler alternative where the client only receives.
Long-lived connections spread across servers; watch for sticky routing needs.
TLS termination and upgrade handling in front of the connection tier.
Stateless apart from its open sockets, so any number can run.
Slow clients must not grow unbounded server-side buffers.
Every server subscribes so a message reaches recipients on other servers.
Presence, room membership and the low-latency pub/sub channel.
The replayable record of every message for history, search and analytics.
Conversation history with ordering and pagination.
Client retries must not duplicate messages; dedupe on a client-generated id.
Push and email for recipients who are not connected.
Message search as a derived index, never the source of truth.
Rolling connection servers requires draining, not killing.
Connection counts, message lag and reconnect storms are the signals that matter.

whenToUse: Users expect updates in well under a second without refreshing
Many clients must see the same event (rooms, documents, dashboards)
Presence, typing indicators or cursors are part of the experience
Message loss is unacceptable even though delivery is asynchronous
tradeoffs: Stateful servers make deploys, autoscaling and failover harder than stateless HTTP
Redis pub/sub is fire-and-forget: it cannot be the only delivery path
Ordering and exactly-once delivery are application problems, not transport features
Connection cost per user is real; idle clients still consume memory and file descriptors
